description: Design a multi-sensor fusion system for autonomous platforms: select sensors by range, resolution, and weather resilience, calibrate the suite, choose a fusion architecture, implement state estimation with Kalman filter variants, and build degradation detection with graceful fallback.

steps.description: Select sensors for the perception stack based on range, resolution, field of view, weather performance, and cost. Compare camera, lidar, radar, ultrasonic, and IMU by their operating envelopes and failure modes.

inputs.name: platform-type
inputs.desc: Type of autonomous platform (ground vehicle, drone, marine, industrial robot)

inputs.name: operating-environment
inputs.desc: Environmental conditions the system must handle (weather, lighting, dust, vibration)

inputs.name: detection-requirements
inputs.desc: Required detection ranges, angular resolution, and object classes

outputs.name: sensor-manifest
outputs.desc: List of selected sensors with specifications, mounting locations, and coverage zones

outputs.name: coverage-gap-analysis
outputs.desc: Identified blind spots and environmental conditions where sensors degrade

process: List detection requirements by range band: near-field (0-10m), mid-field (10-100m), far-field (100m+). For each band, identify which object classes must be detected and at what angular resolution.

Map each sensor modality to its operating envelope. Camera: high resolution but degrades in low light and direct sun; requires ISP tuning per environment. Lidar: precise 3D geometry, degrades in rain/fog/dust proportional to optical density. Radar: weather-immune for velocity and range, poor angular resolution without MIMO or scanning array. Ultrasonic: near-field only, cheap, works in all weather below 10m. IMU: self-contained motion measurement, drifts without external correction.

For each range band, select the primary and backup sensor modality. Primary provides the highest-quality data in nominal conditions. Backup covers the primary's degraded conditions. Every detection requirement must have at least two independent sensor paths.

Define mounting locations from the platform geometry. Each sensor needs clear field of view, vibration isolation appropriate to its sensitivity, thermal management if needed (lidar and camera overheat in sun), and cable routing. Document the coverage map as a polar plot showing sensor footprints overlaid.
Identify remaining coverage gaps and document them as known limitations of the sensor suite. These become inputs to the operational design domain definition.

steps.description: Calibrate the sensor suite: intrinsic parameters for each sensor, extrinsic transforms between all sensor pairs, and temporal synchronization across the suite.

inputs.name: sensor-manifest
inputs.desc: Selected sensors with specifications and mounting locations

inputs.name: coverage-gap-analysis
inputs.desc: Known coverage gaps to verify after calibration

outputs.name: calibration-parameters
outputs.desc: Intrinsic and extrinsic calibration results for every sensor and sensor pair

outputs.name: synchronization-config
outputs.desc: Timing synchronization configuration including trigger scheme and latency compensation

process: Intrinsic calibration for each sensor independently. Camera: checkerboard or ChArUco board, capture 30+ images at varied poses, solve for focal length, principal point, and distortion coefficients (Brown-Conrady model). Verify reprojection error below 0.5 pixels. Lidar: verify point cloud accuracy against known targets at multiple ranges, characterize range bias and angular offset. Radar: measure range and angle accuracy against corner reflectors at known positions. IMU: static bias estimation (gravity alignment), Allan variance analysis for gyro drift and accelerometer noise.

Extrinsic calibration between sensor pairs. Camera-lidar: use a planar target visible to both modalities, solve the rigid body transform (rotation and translation) by minimizing point-to-plane distance in the camera frame. Camera-radar: use corner reflectors with visual fiducials, solve for the 6-DOF transform. Camera-camera: stereo calibration with overlapping checkerboard views. Lidar-IMU: use hand-eye calibration formulation from motion sequences. Verify every transform by projecting one sensor's data into the other's frame and measuring alignment residual.

Temporal synchronization. Determine each sensor's trigger mechanism: hardware trigger (PPS from GPS), software trigger (ROS timestamp), or free-running with timestamp interpolation. Measure the latency from physical event to timestamp for each sensor. Implement a common time base using PTP (IEEE 1588) or GPS PPS. For sensors that cannot be hardware-triggered, measure and compensate for the latency offset. Verify synchronization by recording a fast-moving calibration target and checking cross-sensor temporal alignment.

Validate the full calibration by running a field test with known reference objects. Check that fused data aligns within specification: lidar points project onto camera images within 2-3 pixels, radar detections correspond to lidar clusters within one range resolution cell. Document calibration date, conditions, and residuals for every parameter.

steps.description: Select and design the sensor fusion architecture: early fusion (raw data), mid-level fusion (feature/object level), or late fusion (decision level), based on the system's latency, accuracy, and computational constraints.

inputs.name: calibration-parameters
inputs.desc: Calibrated sensor transforms and timing

inputs.name: sensor-manifest
inputs.desc: Sensor suite with specifications

inputs.name: detection-requirements
inputs.desc: Required detection performance

outputs.name: fusion-architecture
outputs.desc: Selected fusion architecture with data flow diagram, processing stages, and interface definitions

outputs.name: computational-budget
outputs.desc: Processing time allocation per fusion stage and total latency budget

process: Evaluate early fusion: raw data from all sensors projected into a common representation (e.g., bird's-eye-view grid, voxel space). Advantages: the learning model sees everything and can discover cross-modal correlations. Disadvantages: high bandwidth and compute, requires tight synchronization, single model couples all sensor processing. Appropriate when compute is abundant and maximum detection performance justifies the cost.

Evaluate mid-level fusion: each sensor runs its own detection pipeline, outputs are associated and merged at the object or feature level. Camera produces 2D bounding boxes with classification. Lidar produces 3D clusters with geometry. Radar produces tracks with velocity. Association uses gating (Mahalanobis distance in measurement space) then assignment (Hungarian algorithm or GNN). Advantages: modular, each pipeline can run at its own rate, easier to diagnose failures. Disadvantages: association errors, information loss from per-sensor abstraction.

Evaluate late fusion: each sensor produces independent object tracks, a fusion node merges tracks using track-to-track association and covariance intersection or federated filtering. Advantages: simplest integration, sensors can be added or removed without redesign. Disadvantages: loses fine-grained information, association is harder at the track level, latency accumulates through per-sensor tracking.

Select the architecture from the evaluation. In practice, most production systems use mid-level fusion with early-fusion augmentation for critical detections. Define the data flow: sensor drivers, per-sensor processing pipelines, association and fusion node, output object list with uncertainties. Allocate the computational budget: total latency from sensor trigger to fused output must be within the control loop deadline (typically 50-100ms for ground vehicles at highway speed). Assign processing time to each stage.

steps.description: Implement state estimation using Kalman filter variants: select between EKF, UKF, and particle filter based on system nonlinearity and computational constraints, tune process and measurement noise, and validate filter performance.

inputs.name: fusion-architecture
inputs.desc: Selected fusion architecture with data flow

inputs.name: sensor-manifest
inputs.desc: Sensor specifications including noise characteristics

outputs.name: filter-design
outputs.desc: State estimation filter implementation with state vector, process model, measurement models, and noise parameters

outputs.name: filter-performance
outputs.desc: Estimated accuracy of state estimates (position, velocity, orientation) under nominal and degraded conditions

process: Define the state vector. For a ground vehicle: position (x, y), heading, velocity, yaw rate, and optionally acceleration. For a drone: full 6-DOF pose plus velocities. For each tracked object: position, velocity, heading, dimensions, classification. The state vector size determines computational cost per filter update.

Select the filter variant. Extended Kalman Filter (EKF): linearizes nonlinear models around the current estimate using Jacobians. Fast, works well when nonlinearity is mild (small timesteps, smooth motion). Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF): propagates sigma points through the nonlinear model, avoids Jacobian computation, better accuracy for strongly nonlinear systems at 2-3x the cost of EKF. Particle filter: represents the posterior as a set of weighted samples, handles arbitrary nonlinearity and multimodal distributions, but scales poorly with state dimension (practical up to ~10 states with 1000+ particles). For most robotic platforms, EKF or UKF is sufficient for ego-state estimation. Use particle filters for global localization with ambiguous measurements.

Set process noise (Q matrix) and measurement noise (R matrix). Process noise represents unmodeled dynamics: for a constant-velocity model, Q encodes expected acceleration magnitude. Tune Q from recorded trajectory data by computing the innovation sequence and checking its whiteness (autocorrelation should be near zero). Measurement noise R comes from sensor specifications and calibration residuals. Verify consistency: the normalized innovation squared (NIS) should follow a chi-squared distribution with degrees of freedom equal to measurement dimension.

Validate filter performance against ground truth (RTK-GPS for position, motion capture for full pose in controlled environments). Compute RMS error for each state component. Check that the filter's reported covariance (P matrix) is consistent with actual errors: the estimated uncertainty should contain the actual error approximately 95% of the time at the 2-sigma level. Tune Q and R iteratively if consistency is poor.

steps.description: Build sensor health monitoring and graceful degradation: detect when a sensor is providing unreliable data, switch to backup sensor paths, and communicate reduced capability to downstream systems.

inputs.name: filter-design
inputs.desc: State estimation filter with expected measurement residuals

inputs.name: fusion-architecture
inputs.desc: Fusion architecture with sensor data paths

inputs.name: computational-budget
inputs.desc: Processing time allocation

outputs.name: degradation-detection-system
outputs.desc: Sensor health monitoring rules, thresholds, and fallback modes for each sensor

outputs.name: reduced-capability-matrix
outputs.desc: Map of which capabilities are lost when each sensor or sensor combination fails

process: Define health metrics for each sensor. Camera: exposure histogram (saturation or underexposure), blur metric (Laplacian variance), frame drop rate, detection count consistency. Lidar: point count per scan, range noise level, return intensity consistency, self-interference detection. Radar: target count, false alarm rate, SNR trend, interference detection. IMU: bias stability monitoring, vibration spectral content, temperature drift. For each metric, establish normal operating ranges from field data.

Implement per-sensor anomaly detection. Monitor each health metric in a sliding window. Flag a sensor as degraded when any metric exceeds its threshold for more than N consecutive frames (N chosen to avoid false alarms from transient events like passing through a puddle). Flag a sensor as failed when data stops arriving or consistently fails sanity checks (e.g., lidar returns zero points, camera image is black).

Design fallback modes. For each sensor failure combination, define which detection capabilities are retained and which are lost. Single camera failure: switch to adjacent camera or lidar-only detection in that sector. Single lidar failure: camera-based 3D estimation (monocular depth) with degraded range accuracy. Radar failure: lose direct velocity measurement, rely on track-based velocity estimation. IMU failure: rely on visual/lidar odometry with degraded latency response. Document the reduced capability for each failure mode.

Communicate degradation to downstream systems. The sensor fusion module outputs a capability status alongside the fused object list. Downstream planning and control systems use the capability status to adjust their behavior: widen safety margins, reduce speed, limit operational domain. If degradation reduces capability below the minimum for the current operating condition, initiate a transition to a minimal risk condition (e.g., slow down and pull over).

description: Design a motion planning system for autonomous platforms: construct the configuration space, select and implement planning algorithms (sampling-based, optimization-based, lattice), handle dynamic obstacles, enforce comfort and safety constraints, and manage computational budgets for real-time operation.

steps.description: Build the configuration space representation from the platform geometry and environment, transforming the planning problem from workspace to C-space where the robot is a point.

inputs.name: platform-geometry
inputs.desc: Robot dimensions, turning radius, and kinematic constraints

inputs.name: environment-representation
inputs.desc: Map or occupancy grid of the operating environment

inputs.name: planning-requirements
inputs.desc: Speed range, acceleration limits, and mission objectives

outputs.name: c-space-model
outputs.desc: Configuration space representation with obstacle regions, free space, and kinematic constraints encoded

outputs.name: constraint-set
outputs.desc: Complete set of constraints: kinematic, dynamic, safety margins, and comfort bounds

process: Define the configuration space dimensions from the platform kinematics. For a car-like robot: (x, y, theta, velocity) at minimum, optionally steering angle and curvature for smoother planning. For a drone: (x, y, z, yaw) for position planning, full 6-DOF for aggressive maneuvering. For a manipulator: joint angles (N-dimensional C-space). The dimensionality determines which planning algorithms are computationally feasible.

Map workspace obstacles into C-space. For a 2D robot with orientation, compute the Minkowski sum of obstacles with the robot footprint at each orientation. For high-dimensional C-space, explicit computation is impractical; instead sample configurations and collision-check each against the environment using the robot's geometric model. Collision checking is the inner-loop bottleneck; use hierarchical bounding volumes (AABB tree, OBB tree) for speed.

Encode kinematic constraints. Ackermann-steered vehicles have a minimum turning radius that creates non-holonomic constraints: not all C-space directions are reachable from all configurations. Differential-drive robots are also non-holonomic but can turn in place. Holonomic robots (omnidirectional, drones) can move in any direction from any configuration. The constraint type determines which planners are valid: holonomic systems can use any geometric planner, non-holonomic systems need kinodynamic planners or lattice-based planners with pre-computed motion primitives.

Define the constraint set for planning. Kinematic: max velocity, max acceleration, max curvature (from turning radius), max curvature rate (for smooth steering). Dynamic: max lateral acceleration for tire grip, max longitudinal acceleration and braking. Safety: minimum clearance from obstacles (function of speed), minimum time-to-collision threshold. Comfort: max lateral jerk, max longitudinal jerk, max lateral acceleration for passenger comfort (typically 0.2g for normal driving, 0.4g for urgent situations). Document each constraint with its source and rationale.

steps.description: Select and implement the planning algorithm: compare sampling-based (RRT, RRT*, PRM), optimization-based (trajectory optimization, MPC), and lattice planners by the problem structure.

inputs.name: c-space-model
inputs.desc: Configuration space representation

inputs.name: constraint-set
inputs.desc: Kinematic, dynamic, safety, and comfort constraints

inputs.name: planning-requirements
inputs.desc: Real-time deadline, optimality needs, and replanning frequency

outputs.name: planner-implementation
outputs.desc: Selected planning algorithm with parameters, heuristics, and implementation details

outputs.name: performance-characterization
outputs.desc: Expected computation time, path quality, and failure modes for the selected planner

process: Evaluate sampling-based planners. RRT: fast to find any feasible path in high-dimensional spaces, poor path quality (jerky, suboptimal length). RRT*: asymptotically optimal but convergence is slow in practice, rewiring cost grows with sample count. PRM: good for repeated queries in a static environment (roadmap built once), not suitable for dynamic environments. Bidirectional RRT: faster for point-to-point problems. Informed RRT*: uses heuristic to focus sampling, converges faster. Best for: high-dimensional spaces (manipulators), cluttered static environments, when any feasible path is acceptable.

Evaluate optimization-based planners. Trajectory optimization: discretize the trajectory into waypoints, optimize jointly for smoothness, obstacle avoidance, and constraint satisfaction. Can produce high-quality paths but sensitive to initialization (local minima). Model Predictive Control (MPC): optimize over a receding horizon, naturally handles dynamic constraints and replanning, but horizon length limits global reasoning. Best for: structured environments with known dynamics, when path quality matters, when constraints are complex.

Evaluate lattice planners. Pre-compute a library of dynamically feasible motion primitives (short trajectory segments that respect vehicle kinematics). Search over a graph of these primitives using A* or similar. Guarantees kinematic feasibility by construction. Resolution determines path quality and computational cost. Best for: structured driving (roads, parking), when kinematic feasibility is paramount, when the environment has moderate complexity.

Select the planner based on the application. Most production autonomous driving systems use a hierarchical approach: a route planner (A* on road graph) for global planning, a behavior planner (state machine or decision tree) for lane-level decisions, and a local trajectory planner (optimization-based or lattice) for the final smooth trajectory. For manipulators, sampling-based planners with post-optimization smoothing are standard. Document the selected architecture, key parameters (sample count, horizon length, primitive resolution), and the computational budget for each planning layer.

steps.description: Handle dynamic obstacles in motion planning: predict obstacle trajectories, plan around moving objects using velocity obstacles or prediction-aware optimization, and design contingency plans for uncertain behavior.

inputs.name: planner-implementation
inputs.desc: Selected planning algorithm

inputs.name: c-space-model
inputs.desc: Configuration space model

inputs.name: constraint-set
inputs.desc: Safety and comfort constraints

outputs.name: dynamic-planning-system
outputs.desc: Motion planner extended with dynamic obstacle prediction and interaction-aware planning

outputs.name: contingency-plan-framework
outputs.desc: Framework for generating and selecting contingency trajectories when predictions are uncertain

process: Implement obstacle trajectory prediction. Constant velocity prediction: extrapolate current state forward, simple but fails at intersections and lane changes. Physics-based prediction: propagate with a kinematic model, respecting road geometry (vehicles follow lanes). Behavior-aware prediction: classify intent (lane keep, lane change, turn) from observed behavior, predict trajectory per intent hypothesis with probability weights. Interaction-aware prediction: model how the ego vehicle's plan affects other agents' behavior (game-theoretic). Start with physics-based prediction and add behavior awareness where interaction density demands it.

Integrate predictions into planning using velocity obstacles or spatiotemporal planning. Velocity Obstacle (VO): compute the set of ego velocities that would lead to collision with a predicted obstacle trajectory. Plan in velocity space to avoid all VOs. Reciprocal Velocity Obstacles (ORCA): assume all agents share responsibility for avoidance, halves the avoidance burden. Spatiotemporal planning: plan in (x, y, t) space where obstacles sweep out volumes over time, find a path through free spacetime. For optimization-based planners, add obstacle prediction as time-varying constraints.

Design contingency planning for uncertain predictions. Generate multiple trajectory candidates: a nominal trajectory that follows the most likely prediction, and contingency trajectories for alternative obstacle behaviors (e.g., the car ahead brakes hard, the pedestrian steps into the road). Evaluate each contingency for feasibility and cost. Maintain a contingency trajectory that can be executed within the system's reaction time if the nominal plan becomes infeasible. The contingency must always exist; if no safe contingency exists, the system must slow down until one does.

Handle the interaction problem. When the ego vehicle's behavior affects other agents (merging, unprotected left turns, pedestrian crossings), pure prediction-then-plan creates a frozen robot problem: the planner waits for the other agent, who also waits. Break the deadlock by committing to an assertive plan when the situation is safe (sufficient gap), or by communicating intent (turn signal, creeping forward). Tune the assertiveness parameter per scenario: more assertive in dense urban traffic where hesitation creates risk, more conservative near vulnerable road users.

steps.description: Post-process planned trajectories for smoothness, comfort, and constraint satisfaction: apply trajectory smoothing, enforce jerk limits, and verify the final trajectory against all constraints before execution.

inputs.name: dynamic-planning-system
inputs.desc: Planner output including raw trajectory waypoints

inputs.name: constraint-set
inputs.desc: Full constraint set including comfort bounds

outputs.name: executable-trajectory
outputs.desc: Smooth, constraint-satisfying trajectory ready for the control system

outputs.name: constraint-verification-report
outputs.desc: Verification that every constraint is satisfied at every point along the trajectory

process: Apply trajectory smoothing. If the raw planner output is a sequence of waypoints, fit a smooth curve through them. Common approaches: cubic spline interpolation (C2 continuous, fast), quintic polynomial segments (C4 continuous, controls acceleration and jerk), B-spline (adjustable smoothness, convex hull property for obstacle avoidance). Choose the representation that matches the control system's input requirements. For time-parameterized trajectories, smooth position and then compute velocity and acceleration profiles; do not smooth velocity independently as this can create inconsistencies.

Enforce comfort constraints on the smooth trajectory. Check lateral acceleration at every sample point: if it exceeds the comfort limit (typically 2 m/s^2 for normal driving), reduce speed on that segment. Check longitudinal jerk: if it exceeds the limit (typically 1-2 m/s^3), adjust the acceleration profile. Check lateral jerk: if steering changes are too abrupt, increase the transition time. These checks may require iterating between spatial path smoothing and speed profile optimization.

Verify all constraints on the final trajectory. Sample the trajectory at the control loop rate (e.g., every 10ms). At each sample: check collision clearance against static and predicted dynamic obstacles, check kinematic feasibility (curvature within turning radius), check dynamic feasibility (acceleration within tire friction limits), check comfort bounds (jerk, lateral acceleration). If any sample violates a constraint, replan with tighter bounds or flag the trajectory as infeasible.

Prepare the trajectory for execution. Output format: time-stamped sequence of (x, y, heading, curvature, velocity, acceleration) at the control loop rate. Include the constraint verification status and any reduced-confidence flags (e.g., close clearance to obstacles, high predicted curvature near the kinematic limit). The control system uses this trajectory as its reference, tracking it with a path-following controller.

description: Design the perception pipeline for an autonomous system: camera image processing, 3D point cloud analysis, object detection and classification, multi-object tracking, and scene understanding including free space and occupancy mapping.

steps.description: Design the camera processing pipeline from raw sensor data to rectified images: ISP tuning, lens distortion correction, exposure control, and image quality validation.

inputs.name: camera-specifications
inputs.desc: Camera sensor specs including resolution, dynamic range, lens parameters, and frame rate

inputs.name: operating-conditions
inputs.desc: Lighting conditions, weather, and speed range the system must handle

outputs.name: processed-image-stream
outputs.desc: Rectified, exposure-corrected image stream ready for detection algorithms

outputs.name: image-quality-metrics
outputs.desc: Per-frame quality metrics for downstream confidence estimation

process: Configure the image signal processor (ISP). Demosaic the Bayer pattern using an edge-aware algorithm (Malvar-He-Cutler or similar) to minimize color artifacts at edges. Apply white balance calibration per illuminant (D65 for daylight, tungsten for tunnel/garage). Set the tone curve for maximum useful dynamic range rather than aesthetic appearance: preserve detail in shadows and highlights, since detection networks need both. Apply noise reduction conservatively: over-smoothing erases fine texture that distinguishes objects from background.

Implement exposure control for perception. Standard auto-exposure optimizes for average scene brightness, which fails for autonomous driving (dark road with bright headlights, tunnel exit). Instead, use region-weighted exposure: weight the road surface and horizon band more heavily than sky. For HDR: use bracketed exposure with short and long frames, fuse with a deghosting algorithm to prevent motion artifacts. Set exposure limits: minimum exposure time to prevent motion blur at maximum platform speed (e.g., 2ms for highway driving), maximum gain to limit noise.

Apply lens distortion correction. Use the calibrated distortion model (radial and tangential coefficients) to undistort each frame. For wide-angle lenses (common for near-field perception), the barrel distortion is significant and must be corrected before any geometric reasoning. Pre-compute the undistortion map as a lookup table for real-time performance. Verify correction quality by checking that straight lines in the scene appear straight in the corrected image.

Define image quality metrics for each frame. Compute: blur metric (Laplacian variance, threshold below which the frame is flagged), saturation percentage (overexposed or underexposed pixels), noise estimate (from sensor dark areas or flat patches), dynamic range utilization. Attach these metrics to each frame so downstream algorithms can adjust their confidence. A frame with 30% saturation from direct sun glare should reduce detection confidence in the affected region.

steps.description: Process 3D lidar point clouds: ground segmentation, clustering for object detection, and geometric feature extraction.

inputs.name: lidar-specifications
inputs.desc: Lidar specs including point density, range, and scan pattern

inputs.name: processed-image-stream
inputs.desc: Camera data for cross-modal validation

outputs.name: ground-segmented-cloud
outputs.desc: Point cloud with ground points labeled and removed from obstacle detection

outputs.name: object-clusters
outputs.desc: Clustered point groups with bounding boxes, dimensions, and geometric features

process: Ground segmentation. The ground surface must be removed before object clustering to prevent ground points from merging with nearby objects. Methods: RANSAC plane fitting (fast, works for flat ground, fails on hills and curbs), sector-based ground estimation (divide the point cloud into angular sectors, fit a line to the lowest points in each sector, handles slopes), Patchwork/Patchwork++ (ground likelihood estimation per patch, handles uneven terrain). Select based on terrain complexity. Validate by checking that known ground points (road surface) are correctly labeled and known obstacles (curbs, barriers) are not removed.

Cluster non-ground points into object candidates. Euclidean clustering (DBSCAN or connected-components on a voxel grid): set the distance threshold based on point density at the expected detection range. At 50m, lidar points on a car may be 0.5m apart, so the clustering threshold must accommodate this. Problem: under-segmentation (two nearby objects merged) and over-segmentation (one object split across scan lines). Mitigate under-segmentation by using adaptive thresholds that increase with range. Mitigate over-segmentation by using scan-line-aware connectivity.

Extract geometric features from each cluster. Compute: oriented bounding box (minimum-volume OBB from PCA or L-shape fitting), cluster dimensions (length, width, height), point count and density, centroid position, intensity statistics. L-shape fitting is important for vehicles: fit two perpendicular lines to the visible edges to estimate the full vehicle footprint from a partial view. These features feed into classification and tracking.

Cross-validate with camera data. Project each lidar cluster's centroid into the camera image using the calibrated extrinsic transform. Check that the projected position falls within or near a camera detection bounding box. Clusters that have no camera support may be false alarms (ground clutter, vegetation) or objects the camera missed (dark objects, small objects). Use the cross-modal agreement to adjust detection confidence.

steps.description: Select and configure the object detection architecture for camera and lidar: choose between detection paradigms, train or fine-tune models, and optimize for real-time inference on embedded hardware.

inputs.name: detection-requirements
inputs.desc: Required object classes, detection range, and accuracy targets

inputs.name: computational-budget
inputs.desc: Available compute hardware and latency budget for detection

outputs.name: detection-model
outputs.desc: Trained and optimized detection model with architecture, weights, and inference pipeline

outputs.name: detection-performance
outputs.desc: Measured precision, recall, and latency on representative test data

process: Select the detection paradigm. For camera: two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN family) give higher accuracy but more latency; single-stage detectors (YOLO family, SSD) trade some accuracy for speed; anchor-free detectors (CenterNet, FCOS) avoid anchor hyperparameter tuning. For lidar 3D detection: point-based (PointPillars, VoxelNet) encode the point cloud into a pseudo-image and run 2D detection; point-transformer methods give higher accuracy but more compute. For camera-lidar fusion detection: project lidar features onto camera features in BEV space. Select based on the latency budget and accuracy requirements.

Configure the model for the target domain. Adjust input resolution for the range/resolution trade-off: higher resolution detects smaller objects at longer range but increases compute. Set the class list to match detection requirements; adding unnecessary classes wastes capacity. For transfer learning: start from a pretrained backbone (ImageNet or nuScenes/Waymo), fine-tune on domain-specific data. Collect or curate training data that covers the operational design domain: all weather conditions, times of day, object types, and edge cases.

Optimize for embedded inference. Quantize the model from FP32 to INT8 using post-training quantization or quantization-aware training, measuring accuracy loss at each step. Apply TensorRT or equivalent runtime optimization for the target GPU. Profile layer-by-layer to identify bottlenecks. Consider model pruning for further speedup if latency is not met. Target: inference time within the allocated computational budget (e.g., 20ms for a 50ms fusion cycle that includes pre/post-processing).

Validate detection performance. Run evaluation on a held-out test set that represents the operational domain. Report: precision-recall curves per class, AP (average precision) at standard IoU thresholds (0.5, 0.7 for 2D; 0.25, 0.5 for 3D), detection range vs recall curve, inference latency distribution (mean, 95th percentile, max). Identify failure modes: small objects, occluded objects, unusual poses, adverse weather. Document known limitations for the safety case.

steps.description: Implement multi-object tracking: associate detections across frames, manage track lifecycle, and output tracked object states with uncertainty.

inputs.name: detection-model
inputs.desc: Per-frame detection output (bounding boxes, classes, confidence)

inputs.name: object-clusters
inputs.desc: Lidar cluster features for 3D tracking

outputs.name: tracked-objects
outputs.desc: List of tracked objects with ID, state (position, velocity, heading), classification, and uncertainty

outputs.name: tracking-metrics
outputs.desc: Tracking accuracy metrics: MOTA, ID switches, track fragmentation

process: Define the track state and motion model. State: position (x, y, z), velocity (vx, vy), heading, dimensions (length, width, height), classification. Motion model: constant velocity for most objects, bicycle model for vehicles (accounts for turning). Each track maintains a Kalman filter (or UKF for the bicycle model) that predicts the state forward between detections.

Associate detections to tracks using two-stage gating and assignment. First, gate: compute the Mahalanobis distance between each prediction and each detection, reject pairs beyond a threshold (e.g., 99.7% chi-squared gate). Second, assign: use the Hungarian algorithm (optimal assignment) or greedy nearest-neighbor (faster, suboptimal) to match predictions to detections. Cost function: weighted combination of spatial distance, size similarity, and appearance similarity (if using re-identification features). Handle the assignment matrix: matched pairs update their tracks, unmatched detections become tentative new tracks, unmatched predictions increment a missed-detection counter.

Manage track lifecycle. Track states: tentative (new detection, not yet confirmed), confirmed (enough consecutive matches, typically 3-5 frames), lost (missed detections exceeding a threshold, typically 5-10 frames), deleted. Tentative tracks are not reported to downstream systems to avoid false tracks. Confirmed tracks are reported with their full state and uncertainty. Lost tracks continue to predict forward (coasting) and can be re-associated if the object reappears. Delete tracks after the coast timeout to prevent ghost objects.

Output tracked objects with proper uncertainty. Each track reports: unique ID (persistent across frames), state estimate (position, velocity, heading), covariance (uncertainty in each state component), classification with confidence, track age, and time since last detection. Downstream systems use the covariance for decision-making: a track with high positional uncertainty gets a wider safety margin. Measure tracking performance with MOTA (multi-object tracking accuracy), MOTP (precision), ID switch rate, and track fragmentation rate on a validation set.

steps.description: Build scene understanding from tracked objects: free space estimation, occupancy grid mapping, semantic segmentation for drivable area, and scene-level reasoning.

inputs.name: tracked-objects
inputs.desc: Tracked object list with states and uncertainty

inputs.name: ground-segmented-cloud
inputs.desc: Lidar point cloud with ground labeled

inputs.name: processed-image-stream
inputs.desc: Camera image stream for semantic segmentation

outputs.name: scene-model
outputs.desc: Complete scene representation including free space, occupancy grid, drivable area, and lane structure

outputs.name: scene-confidence
outputs.desc: Per-cell confidence in the scene model for planning to use

process: Build the occupancy grid. Discretize the area around the platform into a 2D grid (typical resolution: 0.1-0.2m for parking, 0.5m for highway). For each lidar scan, ray-trace from the sensor through each cell: cells hit by a lidar return are marked occupied, cells the ray passed through are marked free, cells beyond the return are unknown. Update the grid probabilistically using a log-odds formulation (inverse sensor model). The log-odds representation handles repeated observations naturally: cells observed as free many times become confidently free.

Estimate free space from both lidar and camera. Lidar free space: the boundary between the last free cell and the first occupied cell in each radial direction. Camera free space: use a trained network for free space segmentation on the ground plane, project the result into world coordinates using the known camera-ground geometry. Fuse lidar and camera free space estimates: take the more conservative (closer) boundary where they disagree, take either where only one sensor has coverage.

Run semantic segmentation for drivable area. Use a trained segmentation network (DeepLab, SegFormer, or similar) on camera images to classify each pixel: road, sidewalk, lane marking, curb, vegetation, building, sky. Project the road/sidewalk classification onto the ground plane to define the drivable area boundary. Compare with the occupancy grid: the drivable area should be a subset of the free space. Where they disagree, investigate (e.g., occupancy grid shows free space on a sidewalk, but it is not drivable).

Assemble the scene model. Combine: occupancy grid (where things are), free space boundary (where the platform can physically go), drivable area (where the platform is allowed to go), tracked objects (what is moving and where), lane structure (from HD map or lane detection). Output a unified scene representation that the motion planner consumes. Attach confidence to each element: high confidence for cells observed by multiple sensors, lower confidence for single-sensor observations, lowest for extrapolated regions. The planner uses confidence to modulate its safety margins.

description: Design a localization and mapping system for autonomous platforms: select SLAM algorithms, build and maintain maps, implement GPS-denied localization, and validate localization accuracy for safety-critical operation.

steps.description: Select the SLAM algorithm based on sensor suite, environment structure, and accuracy requirements: compare visual SLAM, lidar SLAM, and visual-inertial odometry.

inputs.name: sensor-suite
inputs.desc: Available sensors for localization (cameras, lidar, IMU, GPS)

inputs.name: environment-type
inputs.desc: Indoor/outdoor, structured/unstructured, feature density

inputs.name: accuracy-requirements
inputs.desc: Required position and heading accuracy for the application

outputs.name: slam-architecture
outputs.desc: Selected SLAM approach with algorithm, parameters, and expected performance

outputs.name: map-representation
outputs.desc: Map format and content (point cloud, feature map, occupancy grid, HD map)

process: Evaluate visual SLAM options. ORB-SLAM3: sparse feature-based, works with monocular, stereo, or RGB-D cameras, good loop closure, struggles in textureless environments. LSD-SLAM / DSO: semi-dense or direct methods, work better in low-texture but higher compute. Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO): fuse camera with IMU for robust tracking during fast motion and brief visual dropout (VINS-Mono, MSCKF, OKVIS). VIO is the minimum viable localization for any camera-equipped platform because the IMU bridges gaps in visual tracking.

Evaluate lidar SLAM options. Lidar provides geometric accuracy independent of lighting. LOAM/LeGO-LOAM: extract edge and planar features from lidar scans, match features across scans for odometry, build a feature map. ICP-based (KISS-ICP): register consecutive scans using iterative closest point, simple and effective for high-density lidar. NDT-based: represent the environment as normal distributions in a voxel grid, register scans against the distribution. Lidar SLAM gives centimeter-level accuracy in structured environments but degrades in geometrically repetitive spaces (long tunnels, open fields).

Evaluate fusion approaches. For most outdoor autonomous platforms, the strongest localization combines: lidar SLAM for geometric accuracy, visual features for place recognition (loop closure), IMU for short-term dead reckoning during sensor gaps, GPS for global reference when available. The fusion should be tightly coupled: IMU predictions initialize the scan matching, visual loop closures correct lidar map drift, GPS fixes anchor the map to a global frame.

Select based on the application constraints. Indoor robot with camera only: VIO with sparse visual SLAM. Outdoor vehicle with lidar and camera: lidar SLAM with visual loop closure and IMU integration. Drone in GPS-denied environment: VIO primary, lidar-aided if equipped. Document the selected architecture, expected accuracy (position RMS, heading RMS), and known failure modes (e.g., performance in rain for lidar, in darkness for camera).

steps.description: Build the map from collected sensor data: process mapping runs, optimize the pose graph, generate the map product, and establish quality metrics.

inputs.name: slam-architecture
inputs.desc: Selected SLAM algorithm and configuration

inputs.name: mapping-data
inputs.desc: Raw sensor data from mapping runs (drives, flights, walks)

outputs.name: built-map
outputs.desc: Optimized map with accuracy metadata and coverage documentation

outputs.name: map-quality-report
outputs.desc: Quality metrics: consistency, coverage, accuracy against ground truth

process: Process mapping runs through the SLAM pipeline. Run the selected SLAM algorithm on recorded sensor data. For multi-session mapping: align sessions using common overlap regions, merge into a single consistent map. For large-scale mapping: use hierarchical pose graph optimization (local submaps with global optimization) to manage computational cost. Track the mapping residuals: scan matching scores, feature reprojection errors, GPS consistency. Flag regions where residuals are high for manual review.

Optimize the full pose graph. After all mapping sessions are incorporated, run global pose graph optimization (g2o, GTSAM, or Ceres). Include all constraints: odometry edges, loop closure edges, GPS prior edges. Weight each edge by its measurement uncertainty. After optimization, check for remaining inconsistencies: edges with residuals beyond 3 sigma may indicate incorrect loop closures (perceptual aliasing) and should be reviewed or removed.

Generate the map product. The raw SLAM output (point cloud or feature map) is the localization map. For autonomous driving, enrich with: lane boundaries and lane connectivity (from lidar reflectivity and camera data), traffic signs and signals (geolocated from detection), road surface type, speed limits. This becomes the HD map. For indoor robots: occupancy grid with room labels and semantic annotations. For drones: 3D mesh or elevation map with no-fly zones.

Establish map quality metrics. Absolute accuracy: compare map coordinates to survey-grade ground truth (RTK-GPS control points or total station measurements). Internal consistency: measure the spread of repeat observations of the same feature across sessions. Coverage: verify that every required operating area has sufficient map density for localization. Currency: document the mapping date and change detection methodology for keeping the map updated.

steps.description: Implement real-time localization against the built map: match live sensor data to the map, fuse with IMU and GPS, handle degraded conditions, and output a localization state with uncertainty.

inputs.name: built-map
inputs.desc: Pre-built localization map

inputs.name: slam-architecture
inputs.desc: SLAM algorithm for live matching

outputs.name: localization-system
outputs.desc: Real-time localization pipeline with map matching, sensor fusion, and integrity monitoring

outputs.name: localization-accuracy
outputs.desc: Expected accuracy under nominal and degraded conditions

process: Implement map matching. Load the relevant map section based on approximate position (from GPS or last known position). Match the current sensor observation against the map. For lidar: scan-to-map registration using ICP or NDT with the map as the target. For camera: match extracted features against map features using descriptor matching and PnP pose estimation. The map match provides an absolute position fix with known accuracy (from the map quality metrics).

Fuse map match with dead reckoning. Between map matches, propagate the state using IMU integration (for short periods) or wheel odometry (for ground vehicles). The fusion filter (EKF or factor graph) combines: IMU predictions (high rate, drifts), wheel odometry (medium rate, slip errors), map matches (lower rate, high accuracy), GPS when available (variable accuracy, check consistency before accepting). The filter output is the fused position, heading, and velocity with covariance at the control loop rate.

Handle degraded localization conditions. GPS multipath in urban canyons: detect by checking consistency between GPS and map-matched position, reject GPS fixes that disagree. Lidar degradation in rain or dust: detect by monitoring scan matching score, increase reliance on camera and IMU. Camera degradation in darkness: switch to lidar-primary, increase IMU weight. Total sensor degradation (e.g., dense fog): coast on IMU with growing uncertainty, reduce speed and prepare for controlled stop when uncertainty exceeds the safety threshold.

Monitor localization integrity. The system must know when its position estimate is unreliable. Implement integrity monitoring: compute the protection level (the bound on the position error at a specified confidence level, analogous to GNSS integrity). If the protection level exceeds the alert limit (the maximum tolerable error for safe operation), declare a localization failure and initiate a safe response. Log localization telemetry for offline analysis: position, covariance, sensor availability, matching scores.

steps.description: Validate localization system accuracy and integrity: design test scenarios, measure performance against ground truth, and verify integrity monitoring.

inputs.name: localization-system
inputs.desc: Real-time localization pipeline

inputs.name: accuracy-requirements
inputs.desc: Required accuracy and integrity for the application

outputs.name: validation-results
outputs.desc: Localization accuracy, availability, and integrity performance across test scenarios

outputs.name: known-limitations
outputs.desc: Documented environments and conditions where localization may degrade

process: Design test scenarios covering the operational design domain. Include: nominal conditions (clear weather, good GPS, well-mapped area), GPS-denied (urban canyon, tunnel, indoor), sensor-degraded (rain, fog, night, direct sun), map-change (construction, seasonal vegetation change), dynamic environments (heavy traffic obscuring map features). For each scenario, define the expected localization performance and the acceptance criteria.

Collect ground truth for validation. Use RTK-GPS (centimeter-level, outdoor only), total station (millimeter-level, controlled areas), motion capture (sub-millimeter, indoor only), or a reference trajectory from a higher-grade INS/GPS system. Synchronize ground truth with the localization system's timestamps. The ground truth accuracy must be at least 5x better than the required localization accuracy.

Run validation tests and compute metrics. Position RMS error (lateral, longitudinal, vertical separately). Heading RMS error. 95th and 99th percentile errors. Availability: percentage of time the localization system reports a valid position within the accuracy requirement. Integrity: verify that the protection level computed by the system actually bounds the true error at the specified confidence. Plot the protection level vs actual error over time; the actual error should exceed the protection level less than the specified probability (e.g., 10^-7 per hour for safety-critical applications).

Document known limitations. From the test results, identify environments and conditions where localization degrades. Map these to operational constraints: the system should not operate in environments where localization accuracy cannot meet the safety requirement. Feed these limitations into the operational design domain definition and the safety case.

description: Develop the functional safety case for an autonomous system: perform hazard analysis, assign safety integrity levels, develop the safety concept, analyze SOTIF, define the operational design domain, and construct the safety validation argument.

steps.description: Perform hazard analysis and risk assessment (HARA) for the autonomous system: identify hazards, assess severity, exposure, and controllability, and assign ASIL ratings per ISO 26262.

inputs.name: system-description
inputs.desc: Architecture and functional description of the autonomous system

inputs.name: operational-design-domain
inputs.desc: Environments and conditions the system is intended to operate in

outputs.name: hazard-register
outputs.desc: List of identified hazards with severity, exposure, controllability, and ASIL ratings

outputs.name: safety-goals
outputs.desc: Top-level safety goals derived from the hazards, each with an ASIL rating

process: Identify hazardous events. For each vehicle-level function (longitudinal control, lateral control, perception, localization), consider what happens when the function fails or behaves incorrectly. A failed braking function leads to collision. A failed steering function leads to lane departure. A false detection leads to unnecessary braking. A missed detection leads to collision with an undetected object. Be exhaustive: consider both commission (doing the wrong thing) and omission (failing to do the right thing) for every function.

Assess severity per ISO 26262. S0: no injuries. S1: light to moderate injuries. S2: severe injuries, survival probable. S3: life-threatening, survival uncertain. Assess for the most severe plausible consequence of each hazardous event, considering the operational environment and other road users (pedestrians, cyclists are more vulnerable than other cars).

Assess exposure and controllability. Exposure (E0-E4): how often is the system in the operating scenario where this hazard could occur. Controllability (C0-C3): how likely is the driver or other road users to avoid harm if the hazardous event occurs. For highly automated systems (SAE Level 4+), controllability by the human driver is C3 (uncontrollable) by definition because no driver intervention can be assumed. This pushes most hazards to higher ASIL levels.

Assign ASIL and derive safety goals. Use the ISO 26262 ASIL determination table from S, E, and C ratings. Each hazardous event gets an ASIL (A through D, or QM for no safety requirement). Formulate safety goals as top-level requirements: 'The autonomous driving system shall prevent unintended acceleration' (ASIL D). Each safety goal inherits the ASIL of its parent hazardous event. The safety goals are the starting point for the safety concept.

steps.description: Develop the functional safety concept: decompose safety goals into safety requirements, allocate to system elements, and define the fault detection, indication, and response strategy.

inputs.name: safety-goals
inputs.desc: Top-level safety goals with ASIL ratings

inputs.name: system-description
inputs.desc: System architecture for allocation

outputs.name: safety-requirements
outputs.desc: Functional and technical safety requirements allocated to system elements with ASIL

outputs.name: fault-response-strategy
outputs.desc: For each safety-relevant fault, the detection method, diagnostic coverage, and safe response

process: Decompose safety goals into functional safety requirements (FSR). Each FSR addresses a specific failure mode that could violate the safety goal. Example: safety goal 'prevent unintended acceleration' decomposes into: 'the torque controller shall not command positive torque when the system commands zero torque' (addresses actuator fault), 'the perception system shall not generate false forward clearance when an obstacle exists' (addresses perception fault), 'the planning system shall not generate an acceleration command when the safety goal requires deceleration' (addresses planning fault).

Allocate FSRs to system elements and assign ASIL. ASIL can be decomposed across redundant elements using ASIL decomposition (e.g., ASIL D on a single channel becomes ASIL B(D) + ASIL B(D) on two independent channels). Decomposition requires demonstrated independence between channels (no common-cause failure modes). For software-heavy autonomous systems, achieving ASIL D through decomposition is the practical path because certifying a complex perception stack to ASIL D monolithically is prohibitively expensive.

Define the fault detection and diagnostic strategy. For each safety-relevant element, identify credible faults and design diagnostic tests. Hardware faults: use redundancy (dual-channel lockstep for compute, dual IMUs), built-in self-test (memory ECC, CPU self-test), and plausibility monitoring (compare independent sensor measurements). Software faults: diverse redundancy (different algorithms on different platforms), runtime monitoring (watchdog, execution time monitoring, output range checking). Calculate the diagnostic coverage for each fault type: the fraction of faults that the diagnostic can detect within the fault tolerant time interval.

Define the safe response for each detected fault. The minimal risk condition (MRC) is the state the system transitions to when a fault is detected that cannot be tolerated. For a highway autonomous vehicle, the MRC is typically a controlled stop on the shoulder. The transition to MRC must be achievable within the fault tolerant time interval using only the remaining functional elements. Define degraded operating modes for faults that reduce capability but do not require immediate MRC transition (e.g., single sensor failure with redundant backup).

steps.description: Perform Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF) analysis per ISO 21448: identify performance limitations and triggering conditions that could lead to hazards even without system faults.

inputs.name: safety-requirements
inputs.desc: Functional safety requirements from ISO 26262 analysis

inputs.name: system-description
inputs.desc: Detailed system design including perception and planning algorithms

outputs.name: sotif-analysis
outputs.desc: Triggering conditions, performance limitations, and residual risk assessment for each perception and decision function

outputs.name: sotif-validation-plan
outputs.desc: Plan to demonstrate that residual SOTIF risk is acceptable

process: Identify performance limitations of each function. Perception: maximum detection range by object type and conditions, minimum object size for detection, classification accuracy by class and conditions, false positive and false negative rates. Localization: accuracy degradation in specific environments (tunnels, featureless areas). Planning: scenarios where the planner produces uncomfortable or suboptimal behavior, edge cases in prediction (unusual road user behavior). These are not faults; they are inherent limitations of the algorithms and sensors.

Identify triggering conditions. A triggering condition is a specific scenario that activates a performance limitation and leads to a hazardous behavior. Example: low sun angle (triggering condition) causes camera saturation (performance limitation) leading to missed pedestrian detection (hazardous behavior). Build a triggering condition catalog by systematically combining environmental conditions, road user behaviors, and infrastructure configurations with each known performance limitation.

Classify scenarios into SOTIF areas. Area 1: known safe scenarios (system performs correctly). Area 2: known hazardous scenarios (identified triggering conditions, mitigations in place). Area 3: unknown hazardous scenarios (not yet identified, reduced through testing and analysis). Area 4: unknown safe scenarios. The goal is to minimize Area 3 through systematic exploration: simulation, real-world testing, and expert analysis. No system can eliminate Area 3 entirely; the argument is that it is acceptably small.

Develop the SOTIF validation strategy. Combine: analysis-based methods (systematic triggering condition identification, coverage argument), simulation-based testing (parametric variation of triggering conditions, adversarial scenario generation), real-world testing (mileage-based statistical argument, scenario-based testing at test tracks). The validation target is that the residual risk from SOTIF-related hazards is below the acceptable risk threshold. This threshold comes from the societal risk acceptance framework (e.g., the system must be at least as safe as an attentive human driver).

steps.description: Construct the overall safety validation argument: combine functional safety, SOTIF, and cybersecurity evidence into a structured safety case using Goal Structuring Notation.

inputs.name: safety-requirements
inputs.desc: Functional safety requirements and verification evidence

inputs.name: sotif-analysis
inputs.desc: SOTIF analysis results and validation evidence

inputs.name: hazard-register
inputs.desc: Complete hazard register with mitigations

outputs.name: safety-case
outputs.desc: Structured safety case in GSN with all evidence linked to claims

outputs.name: residual-risk-assessment
outputs.desc: Quantified residual risk and argument that it is acceptable

process: Structure the safety case using Goal Structuring Notation (GSN). Top goal: 'The autonomous system is acceptably safe for operation within the defined ODD.' Decompose into sub-goals: 'All identified hazards are mitigated to an acceptable level' (from HARA), 'The system meets all functional safety requirements' (from ISO 26262), 'SOTIF-related risks are acceptably low' (from ISO 21448), 'The system is resilient to cybersecurity threats' (from ISO 21434).

Link evidence to each claim. For functional safety claims: verification test reports showing each safety requirement is met, diagnostic coverage calculations, FMEA/FTA results, hardware failure rate calculations (PMHF). For SOTIF claims: triggering condition analysis completeness argument, simulation test results, real-world test mileage and encounter statistics, performance monitoring data from field operation. For cybersecurity claims: threat analysis, penetration test results, secure development process evidence.

Assess residual risk. After all mitigations, some risk remains. Quantify it: the probability of a hazardous event occurring per hour of operation, multiplied by the probability that it leads to harm. Compare against the risk acceptance criterion. For automotive: the total residual risk from all autonomous system hazards combined should be below approximately 10^-8 fatalities per hour of operation (comparable to the best human drivers). Document assumptions and limitations in the residual risk calculation.

Identify open items and conditions for deployment. The safety case is never fully complete before deployment; it evolves with field data. Define: conditions that must be met before deployment (all safety requirements verified, SOTIF validation targets met), monitoring requirements during operation (safety-relevant metrics, incident reporting), triggers for safety case update (new failure modes discovered, software updates, ODD expansion). The safety case is a living document maintained throughout the product lifecycle.

description: Design a robot manipulator system: select the kinematic chain, solve kinematics and dynamics, plan trajectories, implement force control, and design the end-effector for the task.

steps.description: Select the manipulator kinematic chain and solve forward and inverse kinematics: choose DOF, extract DH parameters, analyze workspace, and implement IK solutions.

inputs.name: task-requirements
inputs.desc: Workspace volume, payload, reach, dexterity, and speed requirements

inputs.name: mounting-constraints
inputs.desc: Where the manipulator can be mounted and how it can reach the workspace

outputs.name: kinematic-model
outputs.desc: DH parameters, forward kinematics, inverse kinematics solutions, and workspace analysis

outputs.name: manipulator-selection
outputs.desc: Selected manipulator type with DOF, reach, payload, and repeatability specifications

process: Determine the required degrees of freedom from the task. 3 DOF (x, y, z) for pick-and-place without orientation control. 4 DOF for palletizing (x, y, z, plus wrist rotation). 6 DOF for general manipulation (arbitrary position and orientation in 3D). 7+ DOF for redundant manipulators that can reconfigure around obstacles while maintaining end-effector pose. More DOF increases dexterity but also cost, complexity, and control difficulty.

Select the kinematic chain type. Serial (open chain): anthropomorphic (RRR), SCARA (RRP), cylindrical, spherical. Advantages: large workspace relative to footprint, simple kinematics. Disadvantages: cumulative joint errors, lower stiffness. Parallel (closed chain): Delta, Stewart-Gough platform. Advantages: high stiffness, high speed, high accuracy. Disadvantages: small workspace, complex kinematics. Select based on workspace shape, payload, speed, and accuracy requirements.

Extract DH parameters and solve forward kinematics. For the selected chain, assign coordinate frames to each joint using the Denavit-Hartenberg convention. The DH parameters (a, alpha, d, theta) fully specify the kinematic geometry. Forward kinematics: multiply homogeneous transformation matrices from base to end-effector to get the end-effector pose as a function of joint angles. Validate against the manufacturer's specifications or a CAD model.

Solve inverse kinematics. For 6-DOF serial robots, closed-form analytical solutions exist for common configurations (e.g., robots with a spherical wrist: decouple position and orientation). For non-standard configurations or redundant robots, use numerical methods: Jacobian pseudo-inverse (iterative, may converge to local minimum), optimization-based (formulate as nonlinear least squares with joint limit constraints). For redundant robots, use the null-space to optimize a secondary objective (avoid joint limits, avoid obstacles, minimize effort). Verify the IK solution by running FK on the result and checking the pose error is below the repeatability specification.

steps.description: Model the manipulator dynamics for trajectory planning and control: derive the equations of motion, identify inertial parameters, and analyze the dynamic performance envelope.

inputs.name: kinematic-model
inputs.desc: DH parameters and kinematic chain

inputs.name: task-requirements
inputs.desc: Required speeds, accelerations, and payloads

outputs.name: dynamic-model
outputs.desc: Equations of motion with identified inertial parameters (mass, inertia, friction)

outputs.name: torque-requirements
outputs.desc: Joint torque requirements for the task profile, used for motor and gearbox selection

process: Derive the equations of motion. Two standard methods: Lagrangian formulation (compute kinetic and potential energy, derive equations from Euler-Lagrange equations, produces the explicit form M(q)q'' + C(q,q')q' + g(q) = tau) and recursive Newton-Euler (compute forces and torques link by link, computationally efficient for real-time control, O(n) vs O(n^3) for Lagrangian). Use Lagrangian for analysis and understanding, Newton-Euler for implementation.

Identify inertial parameters. From CAD: extract mass, center of mass, and inertia tensor for each link including the motor and gearbox at each joint. From experiments: use excitation trajectories (trajectories that excite all dynamic parameters) and measure joint torques, then solve a least-squares problem for the parameter set. Experimental identification captures friction and compliance that CAD misses. Include viscous friction (proportional to velocity) and Coulomb friction (constant magnitude, direction depends on velocity sign) at each joint.

Analyze the dynamic performance envelope. Compute the maximum end-effector acceleration and velocity achievable at each workspace point, considering joint torque limits and gear ratios. Identify configurations where the manipulator is near a singularity (the Jacobian loses rank, certain end-effector directions require infinite joint velocities). Map the manipulability measure (determinant or condition number of the Jacobian) across the workspace. This shows where the robot can move agilely and where it is sluggish or singular.

Determine joint motor and gearbox requirements. For each joint, compute the peak and RMS torque from the task trajectory profile (including payload, acceleration, and gravity). Select the motor to meet RMS torque at continuous rating and peak torque at intermittent rating. Select the gear ratio to match motor speed to joint speed; higher ratio reduces motor torque requirement but adds backlash and inertia. Check that reflected motor inertia through the gear ratio does not dominate the link inertia (gear ratio squared effect).

steps.description: Plan manipulator trajectories in joint space and Cartesian space: generate smooth motion profiles, handle via points, and respect velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits.

inputs.name: kinematic-model
inputs.desc: Kinematics including IK solutions

inputs.name: dynamic-model
inputs.desc: Dynamic limits (max velocity, acceleration, torque per joint)

inputs.name: task-requirements
inputs.desc: Task waypoints, cycle time requirements, and path constraints

outputs.name: trajectory-plan
outputs.desc: Time-parameterized trajectory (joint angles or Cartesian pose vs time) with velocity and acceleration profiles

outputs.name: cycle-time-analysis
outputs.desc: Achievable cycle time and bottleneck identification

process: Choose between joint-space and Cartesian-space planning. Joint-space: interpolate between joint configurations, simple and fast, guarantees joint limit compliance, but the end-effector path in Cartesian space is not controlled (may swing unexpectedly). Cartesian-space: specify the end-effector path (e.g., straight line, arc), solve IK at each trajectory point, guarantees a predictable Cartesian path, but may encounter singularities and joint limit issues. Use Cartesian-space for tasks requiring precise paths (welding, painting, machining). Use joint-space for point-to-point moves (pick and place).

Generate smooth motion profiles. Trapezoidal velocity profile: accelerate, cruise, decelerate. Simple, time-optimal for a given acceleration limit, but has discontinuous acceleration (jerk is infinite at transitions). S-curve (7-segment) profile: adds jerk-limited transition segments, smoother for mechanical systems and reduces vibration excitation. Polynomial (3rd, 5th, 7th order): fits start and end conditions (position, velocity, acceleration) exactly, higher order gives more smoothness but may oscillate.

Handle via points. For a sequence of waypoints, options: stop at each via point (trapezoidal profiles between each pair, easy but slow due to deceleration and re-acceleration), blend through via points (insert circular or polynomial blends near each via point to maintain speed, faster cycle time). For blended via points, the blend radius trades off between path accuracy at the via point and speed. In joint space, blend in each joint independently.

Verify the trajectory against all limits. At each time step: check joint positions against joint limits, check joint velocities against motor speed limits, check joint accelerations against torque limits (using the inverse dynamics model), check Cartesian velocity and acceleration against task requirements. If any limit is violated, scale the trajectory time (slower) or modify the path. Compute the cycle time and identify the bottleneck (which joint or which path segment limits the overall speed). Optimize by adjusting via point locations or blend radii to reduce the bottleneck.

steps.description: Implement force control for contact tasks: select between impedance and admittance control, design the interaction controller, and handle the transition between free motion and contact.

inputs.name: dynamic-model
inputs.desc: Manipulator dynamics model

inputs.name: task-requirements
inputs.desc: Contact task specification (assembly, grinding, polishing, insertion)

outputs.name: force-controller
outputs.desc: Interaction control system with parameters tuned for the task

outputs.name: contact-transition-logic
outputs.desc: Logic for detecting contact and switching between free-motion and force-control modes

process: Select the force control strategy. Impedance control: the robot behaves like a mass-spring-damper system. Command a desired impedance (stiffness, damping) rather than a desired force. Good for unknown or varying contact geometry. The robot naturally accommodates geometric uncertainty because it yields in contact. Requires accurate dynamic model and joint torque control (or backdrivable actuators). Admittance control: measure the contact force, compute the corresponding velocity or position adjustment. Works with position-controlled robots (most industrial robots). Less natural interaction dynamics but easier to implement on standard hardware.

Design the impedance/admittance parameters for the task. For assembly (peg-in-hole): low stiffness in the insertion direction (to accommodate alignment error), high stiffness perpendicular (to maintain alignment). For grinding/polishing: constant force normal to the surface (force control in one direction), position control tangent to the surface (to follow the path). Hybrid position/force control: partition the task space into force-controlled and position-controlled directions using a selection matrix. Tune stiffness and damping by starting conservative (soft, well-damped) and increasing stiffness until the task performance (speed, accuracy) meets requirements without instability.

Handle the free-motion to contact transition. In free motion, the robot moves to the approach pose under pure position control. Detect contact onset: monitor force/torque sensor or joint torque residuals for a threshold crossing. At contact detection, switch to the force-controlled mode. The transition must be smooth to avoid impact forces: reduce approach velocity as the robot nears the expected contact point, and enable a compliant mode before contact. After the task, detect loss of contact and switch back to position control for retraction.

Address practical force control challenges. Sensor noise: force/torque sensors pick up vibration and gravity compensation errors; filter the force signal (low-pass, but not so much that the control loop is too slow). Gravity compensation: compute and subtract the gravitational torques on the wrist-mounted force sensor from the robot's known pose and payload mass. Environment stiffness: very stiff environments (metal-on-metal contact) make force control difficult because small position errors create large forces; reduce control stiffness or use a compliant tool adapter. Stability: the coupled robot-environment system can become unstable if the controller bandwidth exceeds the environment's natural frequency; analyze and limit bandwidth accordingly.

description: Design an autonomous drone system: select the airframe, size the propulsion, design the flight controller, plan autonomous missions, implement sense-and-avoid, and address regulatory requirements.

steps.description: Select the airframe type and size the propulsion system: match the platform to the mission profile, select motors and propellers, and calculate endurance from battery energy.

inputs.name: mission-profile
inputs.desc: Mission type (inspection, survey, delivery, surveillance), payload mass, endurance requirement, operating environment

inputs.name: performance-requirements
inputs.desc: Max speed, climb rate, wind resistance, and operating altitude

outputs.name: airframe-design
outputs.desc: Selected airframe type with configuration, dimensions, and mass breakdown

outputs.name: propulsion-system
outputs.desc: Motor, propeller, ESC, and battery selection with performance curves and endurance calculation

process: Select the airframe type from the mission profile. Multirotor (quad, hex, octo): vertical takeoff and landing, hover capability, simple control, but low endurance (20-40 min typical) and low cruise efficiency. Best for: inspection, photography, short-range delivery, indoor operation. Fixed-wing: high endurance (1-4 hours), long range, efficient cruise, but cannot hover and needs space for takeoff and landing. Best for: mapping, survey, long-range surveillance. VTOL hybrid (tilt-rotor, tail-sitter, quadplane): combines hover capability with efficient cruise, complex mechanically and aerodynamically. Best for: missions needing both hover and long range.

Size the propulsion for multirotor. Start from the all-up weight (airframe + battery + payload + propulsion). The thrust-to-weight ratio at hover determines efficiency; design for hover at 50-60% throttle (TWR ~2:1) for maneuverability margin and efficiency. Select the propeller diameter from the frame size. Match the motor KV (rpm/volt) to the propeller: low KV for large props (efficient hover), high KV for small props (agile). From the motor and propeller thrust curve, verify thrust at hover throttle, maximum thrust for climb and wind resistance, and power consumption at hover.

Calculate endurance from battery energy. Battery energy (Wh) = capacity (Ah) * nominal voltage (V). Hover power = all-up weight (N) * disk loading correction. Endurance = battery energy / hover power * discharge efficiency (typically 80% usable). For fixed-wing: calculate cruise power from drag at cruise speed (drag = 0.5 * rho * V^2 * S * Cd), endurance = battery energy / cruise power. Account for reserve (typically 20% for safe return). The endurance calculation is the primary constraint driving the battery-payload trade-off.

Complete the mass breakdown and verify closure. Sum: airframe structure (30-40% of AUW for multirotor), propulsion (motors, ESCs, 15-20%), battery (30-40%), payload (given), avionics (GPS, flight controller, telemetry, 5-10%). Verify the total equals the all-up weight assumed in propulsion sizing. Iterate if not: a heavier battery gives more endurance but increases the weight that the motors must lift, diminishing returns. Plot endurance vs battery mass to find the optimum.

steps.description: Design the flight controller: cascaded attitude and rate control loops, state estimation from IMU and GPS, and failsafe behaviors.

inputs.name: airframe-design
inputs.desc: Airframe configuration, dimensions, and inertia estimates

inputs.name: propulsion-system
inputs.desc: Motor response characteristics and thrust mapping

outputs.name: flight-controller
outputs.desc: Control architecture with PID gains, state estimator configuration, and mixer matrix

outputs.name: failsafe-design
outputs.desc: Failsafe behaviors for GPS loss, RC link loss, low battery, and motor failure

process: Design the cascaded control architecture. Outer loop (position controller): takes desired position and velocity, outputs desired attitude angles and thrust. Runs at 50-100 Hz. Middle loop (attitude controller): takes desired roll, pitch, yaw angles, outputs desired angular rates. Runs at 250-500 Hz. Inner loop (rate controller): takes desired angular rates, outputs motor commands through the mixer. Runs at 250-1000 Hz. The cascaded structure allows each loop to be tuned independently with increasing bandwidth from outer to inner.

Tune PID controllers for each loop. Rate loop (innermost): dominates the handling quality. Start with P gain, increase until oscillation, back off 30%. Add D gain to damp oscillation. Add I gain to eliminate steady-state error from motor/prop imbalance. Attitude loop: P gain only (D is provided by the rate loop). Position loop: P gain for position hold stiffness, I for wind rejection, D for velocity damping. Tune in this order (inner first) because inner loop dynamics affect outer loop response. Use step response tests for rate and attitude loops, figure-8 flight for position loop.

Configure the state estimator. Fuse IMU (gyroscope and accelerometer) with GPS, magnetometer, and barometer using an EKF. Gyroscope: primary angular rate measurement, integrate for attitude between correction updates. Accelerometer: measures gravity direction for roll/pitch correction (unreliable during maneuvers, so reduce weight when acceleration is far from 1g). Magnetometer: heading reference, susceptible to magnetic interference (calibrate hard and soft iron, reduce weight near metal structures). GPS: position and velocity, 5-10 Hz update rate, 1-3m accuracy. Barometer: altitude, high-rate but affected by pressure changes and prop wash. Fuse with appropriate noise models for each sensor.

Design failsafe behaviors. GPS loss: hold position using last known GPS position with increasing uncertainty, land if GPS does not recover within timeout. RC link loss: execute return-to-launch at a safe altitude, land after a timeout, or continue the autonomous mission if configured. Low battery: alert, return-to-launch, forced landing at critical voltage to prevent damage. Motor failure: for hexacopter or octocopter, redistribute thrust to remaining motors (controllability analysis determines minimum motor count for each DOF). For quadcopter, a single motor failure means loss of yaw control; descend in controlled spin. Define the priority: land safely above all else.

steps.description: Plan autonomous drone missions: waypoint generation, survey pattern design, corridor planning, geofencing, and dynamic replanning.

inputs.name: mission-profile
inputs.desc: Mission objectives, area of interest, and constraints

inputs.name: airframe-design
