inputs.desc: Platform endurance, speed, and altitude capabilities

inputs.name: flight-controller
inputs.desc: Flight controller capabilities and limitations

outputs.name: mission-plan
outputs.desc: Complete mission plan with waypoints, altitudes, speeds, and camera/sensor actions at each point

outputs.name: contingency-plans
outputs.desc: Alternative plans for weather abort, battery margin, and airspace changes

process: Generate the mission plan from objectives. Survey mission: compute a lawnmower or serpentine pattern over the area of interest. Line spacing from camera footprint at altitude: GSD (ground sample distance) = pixel size * altitude / focal length. Overlap requirement (typically 70% forward, 60% side for photogrammetry) determines the line spacing and trigger interval. Inspection mission: generate waypoints at inspection points with specific viewing angles. Corridor mission (pipeline, powerline): follow the corridor centerline with cross-track waypoints for complete coverage.

Apply operational constraints. Altitude: minimum altitude for obstacle clearance, maximum altitude from regulation (400 ft AGL in US under Part 107) or airspace restriction. Speed: maximum speed for image quality (motion blur limit from exposure time and GSD), minimum speed for wind resistance (ground speed must be positive in worst-case wind). Geofence: define the boundary the drone must not cross, with a buffer for control authority. No-fly zones: restrict overflights of people, roads, or restricted areas. Battery: plan the return-to-launch with sufficient reserve from any point in the mission.

Optimize the flight path for efficiency. For survey patterns: orient the flight lines along the longest dimension of the area to minimize the number of turns (turns waste time and battery). Start from the downwind side so the return leg is faster. For multi-battery missions: plan each sortie to minimize the number of redundant overlap strips between sorties. For delivery or inspection: solve the traveling salesman problem variant for the optimal visit order.

Design contingency plans. Weather abort: monitor wind speed and precipitation, define thresholds for mission continue/abort based on the platform's wind resistance capability. If aborted mid-mission, log the completed coverage and generate a resume plan for the remaining area. Low battery contingency: at any point during the mission, the shortest safe path to a landing zone must be within the remaining battery capacity; if not, begin return immediately. Airspace conflict: if a manned aircraft is detected or ATC issues a restriction, execute a hold or descend pattern until clearance.

steps.description: Implement sense-and-avoid for drone operations: detect and track airborne and ground obstacles, compute collision risk, and execute avoidance maneuvers.

inputs.name: mission-plan
inputs.desc: Planned flight path and operational area

inputs.name: airframe-design
inputs.desc: Platform maneuverability and sensor payload capacity

outputs.name: detect-and-avoid-system
outputs.desc: Obstacle detection, tracking, collision risk assessment, and avoidance maneuver design

outputs.name: regulatory-compliance-package
outputs.desc: Documentation showing compliance with detect-and-avoid requirements for BVLOS operations

process: Select detection sensors for the operating environment. Cooperative: ADS-B In receiver detects transponder-equipped aircraft (most manned aircraft above 18,000 ft, increasingly at lower altitudes). FLARM for general aviation and gliders in some regions. Non-cooperative: radar (detects aircraft without transponders, works in all weather, heavy and power-hungry), camera-based detection (lightweight, detects against sky background using contrast, limited range in poor visibility, requires specialized tracking algorithms for small targets against cluttered backgrounds), lidar (limited range for air-to-air, more useful for ground obstacles during low-altitude operations). Most BVLOS operations require both cooperative and non-cooperative detection.

Implement obstacle tracking and collision risk assessment. Track detected obstacles using a Kalman filter with a constant-velocity or constant-turn model. Compute the closest point of approach (CPA): project both the drone's and the obstacle's trajectories forward, find the time and distance of minimum separation. If the projected CPA is within the collision avoidance threshold (well clear volume: 2000 ft horizontally, 250 ft vertically for integration with manned aviation, or smaller for small UAS operations), initiate avoidance. Assess urgency from time to CPA: advisory (>60s), corrective (35-60s), warning (<35s).

Design avoidance maneuvers. Follow the right-of-way rules: drones yield to all manned aircraft. Preferred avoidance direction: horizontal (right turn in head-on, right turn away in converging), or vertical (descend if the intruder is above, climb if below, matching manned aircraft convention). The avoidance maneuver must clear the well-clear volume and return to the planned path after the conflict is resolved. For ground obstacles during low-altitude flight: maintain a minimum clearance altitude, use lidar or camera-based terrain following.

Prepare the regulatory compliance package. For BVLOS operations in the US, an FAA waiver requires demonstrating: the ability to detect and avoid other aircraft (equivalent level of safety to visual line of sight), a plan to mitigate risk to people on the ground (ground risk buffer or population density constraints), operational procedures for lost link, low battery, and weather. Document: detection sensor specifications and tested detection range, tracking filter performance, avoidance maneuver response time, and field test results demonstrating the system detects and avoids intruder aircraft.

description: Design a control system from scratch: identify the plant from data, build a model, design and tune the controller, analyze stability and robustness, implement in discrete time, and validate the closed-loop performance.

steps.description: Identify the plant dynamics from experimental data: design excitation signals, collect response data, and extract transfer function or state-space models.

inputs.name: plant-description
inputs.desc: Physical system to be controlled, including actuators and sensors

inputs.name: performance-requirements
inputs.desc: Required bandwidth, settling time, steady-state accuracy, and disturbance rejection

outputs.name: plant-model
outputs.desc: Identified plant model (transfer function or state-space) with uncertainty bounds

outputs.name: model-validation
outputs.desc: Validation results showing model accuracy on test data not used for identification

process: Design the excitation signal. The signal must excite the plant across the frequency range of interest (from DC to at least 5x the desired control bandwidth). Options: step input (simple, reveals DC gain and dominant time constant), frequency sweep (sine wave with slowly increasing frequency, directly yields the Bode plot), pseudo-random binary sequence (PRBS: broadband excitation, efficient, good for linear system identification), multisine (sum of sinusoids at selected frequencies, controls the frequency content precisely). Choose amplitude to stay within the linear operating range.

Collect and preprocess data. Sample the input and output at a rate at least 10x the highest frequency of interest (Nyquist with margin). Remove DC offset if needed. Apply anti-aliasing filter before sampling. For frequency response identification: compute the FFT of input and output, divide output spectrum by input spectrum to get the frequency response H(jw). For time-domain identification: use the input-output time series directly.

Extract the model. Frequency domain: fit a transfer function (poles and zeros) to the measured frequency response using least-squares in the frequency domain, weighting by data quality. Start with a low-order model and increase order until the fit is adequate. Time domain: use prediction error methods (PEM) or subspace identification (N4SID) to fit a state-space model to the input-output data. Select model order using information criteria (AIC, BIC) or by examining the singular values in the subspace method.

Validate the model. Split the data: use one portion for identification, another for validation. On the validation data, simulate the model with the measured input and compare the simulated output to the measured output. Compute the fit percentage (NRMSE). A good model should achieve >80% fit on validation data. Also compare the model's frequency response to the measured frequency response: they should agree within the frequency range of interest. Document the model's valid frequency range and amplitude range.

steps.description: Design the controller: select the control architecture, tune PID or state-feedback gains, and ensure the controller meets performance specifications.

inputs.name: plant-model
inputs.desc: Identified plant model with uncertainty

inputs.name: performance-requirements
inputs.desc: Bandwidth, settling time, overshoot, and disturbance rejection requirements

outputs.name: controller-design
outputs.desc: Controller transfer function or gain matrices with all parameters

outputs.name: predicted-performance
outputs.desc: Simulated closed-loop performance against specifications

process: Select the control architecture. SISO with PID: for plants with a single dominant mode, PID is sufficient and well-understood. P for speed, I for steady-state accuracy, D for damping. Lead-lag compensation: for plants needing phase boost at crossover (lead) or low-frequency gain increase (lag). MIMO state feedback (LQR): for multi-input-multi-output systems, optimal for balancing response speed against control effort. State feedback with observer (LQG): when not all states are measurable, design a Kalman filter to estimate them. Select the simplest architecture that meets the specifications.

Design PID controller from the plant model. Method 1 (loop shaping): plot the open-loop Bode plot, design the controller to shape it: crossover frequency sets bandwidth (choose based on settling time: bandwidth ~ 4/settling_time), slope of -20 dB/decade at crossover for stability, add phase lead (D term) if the plant phase is too negative at crossover, add lag (I term) for low-frequency gain. Method 2 (pole placement): specify desired closed-loop poles from the performance requirements (natural frequency from bandwidth, damping ratio from overshoot), compute PID gains that place the closed-loop poles there. Method 3 (optimization): minimize a cost function (e.g., ITAE) over the PID gains with constraints on overshoot and settling time.

Design LQR state feedback (for multi-input or high-order systems). Form the cost function J = integral(x'Qx + u'Ru)dt. Q weights the state errors: larger Q penalizes deviation from the setpoint more, giving faster response. R weights the control effort: larger R gives smoother control inputs. Start with Q = C'C (penalizes output error) and R = I (equal penalty on all inputs). Solve the algebraic Riccati equation for the optimal gain K. Simulate the closed-loop response. Adjust Q and R to meet specifications: if too slow, increase Q; if control is too aggressive, increase R. If not all states are measurable, design a Kalman filter (observer) with the same model and measurement noise characteristics.

Simulate the closed-loop performance. Apply: step reference (check rise time, overshoot, settling time, steady-state error), step disturbance (check rejection speed and steady-state), noise on the measurement (check that high-frequency controller action is acceptable). Verify all specifications are met. If not, iterate on the controller design. Check actuator saturation: simulate with realistic actuator limits and verify the closed-loop does not wind up (add anti-windup for PID) or become unstable.

steps.description: Analyze the closed-loop stability and robustness: compute stability margins, assess sensitivity to model uncertainty, and verify robustness to parameter variation.

inputs.name: controller-design
inputs.desc: Controller with all parameters

inputs.name: plant-model
inputs.desc: Plant model with identified uncertainty

outputs.name: stability-analysis
outputs.desc: Gain margin, phase margin, delay margin, and sensitivity function analysis

outputs.name: robustness-assessment
outputs.desc: Robustness to parameter variation, unmodeled dynamics, and time delay

process: Compute classical stability margins. Gain margin: the factor by which the loop gain can increase before instability. Minimum 6 dB (factor of 2) for industrial systems, 12 dB for safety-critical. Phase margin: the phase lag that can be added before instability. Minimum 30 degrees for industrial, 45 degrees for safety-critical. Delay margin: the time delay that can be added before instability; compute from phase margin / crossover frequency. Plot the Nyquist diagram and verify the encirclement count matches the expected number of unstable open-loop poles.

Analyze the sensitivity functions. Sensitivity S = 1/(1+L): the transfer function from disturbance to output. Complementary sensitivity T = L/(1+L): the transfer function from reference to output (and from noise to output). |S| + |T| = 1 at every frequency (approximately). The peak of |S| (Ms) indicates robustness: Ms < 2 (6 dB) is a common requirement; higher peaks indicate near-instability. The peak of |T| (Mt) indicates noise amplification. Plot S and T on Bode plots; the crossover frequency where |S| = |T| = -3 dB is the bandwidth.

Assess robustness to plant uncertainty. Vary the plant parameters within their identification uncertainty bounds (e.g., +/-20% on gain, +/-10% on time constants). Re-compute the closed-loop response and stability margins for each variation. If stability margins drop below the minimum at any parameter combination, the controller is not robust. Use structured singular value (mu analysis) for a rigorous bound on the worst-case uncertainty combination. Alternatively, Monte Carlo simulation with parameter distributions gives a probabilistic robustness assessment.

Test robustness to unmodeled dynamics. The identified plant model omits high-frequency dynamics (resonances, sensor dynamics, actuator bandwidth). Model these as multiplicative uncertainty: the true plant is G_true = G_model * (1 + delta * W(s)) where W(s) is a weighting function that increases with frequency (unmodeled dynamics are larger at high frequencies) and |delta| <= 1. The robust stability condition is |T * W| < 1 at all frequencies. This sets an upper limit on the controller bandwidth: if you push the bandwidth too high, the controller becomes sensitive to unmodeled dynamics.

steps.description: Implement the controller in discrete time for digital execution: select the sample rate, discretize the controller, handle computational delay, and validate on the real hardware.

inputs.name: controller-design
inputs.desc: Continuous-time controller design

inputs.name: stability-analysis
inputs.desc: Stability margins and robustness bounds

inputs.name: plant-description
inputs.desc: Hardware platform for implementation

outputs.name: discrete-controller
outputs.desc: Discrete-time controller implementation with sample rate, anti-aliasing, and computational delay compensation

outputs.name: hardware-validation
outputs.desc: Closed-loop performance measured on real hardware against specifications

process: Select the sample rate. Minimum: 10x the controller bandwidth (Nyquist with margin for the closed-loop dynamics). Higher rates reduce discretization error but increase computational load. For most electromechanical systems, 1-10 kHz. For thermal or process control, 1-100 Hz. Verify that the computing platform can execute the control algorithm within one sample period. Implement an anti-aliasing filter on the sensor input: a low-pass filter with cutoff at the Nyquist frequency (half the sample rate), typically a second-order Butterworth.

Discretize the controller. Methods: Tustin (bilinear) transform: preserves frequency response well, the standard choice. Zero-order hold: matches the step response, appropriate when the control signal is held constant between samples. Matched pole-zero: places discrete poles and zeros at the mapped locations of the continuous ones. For PID: discretize each term. P is trivial. I becomes a running sum (use trapezoidal integration for accuracy). D becomes a difference equation with a low-pass filter to limit high-frequency gain (filtered derivative: D(z) = Kd * N * (1 - z^-1) / (1 + N*Ts/2 * (1 + z^-1)/(1 - z^-1)) approximately). Verify the discrete controller's frequency response matches the continuous design at frequencies below Nyquist/4.

Handle computational delay. The controller reads the sensor, computes the output, and applies it to the actuator. This takes time (one sample period in the simplest case). Model the delay as z^-1 in the loop. Recompute stability margins with the delay included. If margins are insufficient, either increase the sample rate (reduce the delay as a fraction of the dynamics) or add a Smith predictor (model-based delay compensation). For cascaded loops, ensure the inner loop executes and settles within the outer loop's sample period.

Validate on hardware. Deploy the discrete controller to the real system. Run the same tests as in simulation: step response, disturbance rejection, noise sensitivity. Compare hardware results to simulated predictions. Common discrepancies: actuator saturation or rate limiting not in the model, sensor noise higher than modeled, unmodeled resonances excited at the chosen bandwidth. Iterate: if the hardware performance does not match simulation, refine the plant model with the new data and redesign. Document the final controller parameters, sample rate, and measured performance.

description: Design a simulation and validation framework for autonomous systems: build the simulator, model sensors and physics, generate test scenarios, and construct the statistical safety argument.

steps.description: Design the simulator architecture: select the physics engine, sensor models, and environment representation, and define the simulation fidelity requirements.

inputs.name: system-under-test
inputs.desc: The autonomous system to be validated, with its interfaces

inputs.name: validation-objectives
inputs.desc: What the simulation must demonstrate (safety, performance, robustness)

outputs.name: simulator-design
outputs.desc: Simulator architecture with component selection, fidelity levels, and interface definitions

outputs.name: fidelity-requirements
outputs.desc: Required simulation fidelity for each component to achieve valid test results

process: Define the simulation loop. The simulator replaces the real world: it provides sensor data to the autonomous system and receives control commands back. The simulation loop: update physics (vehicle dynamics, other actors), render sensor data (camera images, lidar point clouds, radar returns), deliver sensor data to the system under test, receive and apply control commands, advance time. The loop rate must match the real-time sensor rates or run faster for accelerated testing.

Select the physics engine. Vehicle dynamics: bicycle model (fast, adequate for normal driving), multi-body dynamics (accurate suspension, tire, and chassis modeling for aggressive maneuvers), or lookup-table from real vehicle testing (highest accuracy, limited to the tested vehicle). Other actors: replay recorded trajectories (deterministic, limited coverage), reactive agents (respond to the ego vehicle, more realistic), or learned behavior models. Environment: static from HD map or 3D scan, dynamic elements (traffic lights, construction zones) from scenario scripts.

Design sensor models at appropriate fidelity. Camera: physically-based rendering (ray tracing for accurate lighting, reflections, and lens effects) gives the most realistic images but is computationally expensive. Reduced fidelity: rasterized rendering with post-processing for noise and blur. Minimum: sensor noise model applied to ground-truth detections (skip image rendering entirely for fast testing of planning and control). Lidar: ray casting against the 3D scene with noise, beam divergence, and multi-return modeling. Radar: point target model with range, Doppler, and cross-section, plus clutter generation. Match fidelity to the test objective: perception testing needs high-fidelity sensor models, planning testing can use ground-truth perception with injected errors.

Define the domain gap management strategy. No simulator perfectly matches reality. Identify the differences: visual appearance (rendering vs real images), physics (simplified dynamics vs real tire behavior), sensor noise (modeled vs actual statistical distribution), actor behavior (scripted vs human drivers). For each gap, either reduce it (improve the model) or account for it (validate that the gap does not invalidate the test results). Transfer learning: test in simulation for coverage, validate on real-world data for accuracy. Document the domain gaps and their impact on test validity.

steps.description: Generate test scenarios systematically: cover the operational design domain, create adversarial scenarios, and mine real-world data for edge cases.

inputs.name: simulator-design
inputs.desc: Simulator with its capabilities and fidelity

inputs.name: validation-objectives
inputs.desc: What to test and acceptance criteria

outputs.name: scenario-library
outputs.desc: Structured library of test scenarios with coverage documentation

outputs.name: scenario-generation-pipeline
outputs.desc: Automated pipeline for generating new scenarios from data or parametric variation

process: Define the scenario description framework. Each scenario specifies: initial conditions (ego pose, speed, other actors), environment (road geometry, weather, lighting, traffic signs/signals), actor behaviors over time (trajectories, decision points), and the expected outcome (pass criteria). Use a scenario description language (OpenSCENARIO or similar) for machine-readable specification. Categorize scenarios by type: nominal (common driving situations), edge (rare but plausible), adversarial (designed to exploit known weaknesses).

Generate parametric scenario variations. Take each base scenario and vary its parameters: actor speeds, gaps, positions, timing. Use methods: grid search (exhaustive but expensive), Latin hypercube sampling (space-filling with fewer samples), adaptive sampling (focus on the boundary between pass and fail regions). For each scenario type, define the relevant parameter ranges from the operational design domain. Example: for a cut-in scenario, vary the cut-in speed, gap, and lateral rate across their plausible ranges.

Mine real-world data for edge cases. From fleet driving data or public datasets, extract scenarios where the system or a human driver encountered difficulty: hard braking events, near-misses, unusual road user behavior, adverse weather encounters. Replay these in simulation to verify the system handles them correctly. Cluster similar events and create representative scenarios. This data-driven approach finds scenarios that parametric variation might miss because they involve combinations of factors not predicted analytically.

Generate adversarial scenarios. Use optimization to find the scenario parameters that maximize the system's failure probability. Methods: gradient-based optimization if the simulator is differentiable, evolutionary algorithms for black-box optimization, reinforcement learning to train adversarial agents that provoke failures. Adversarial testing is valuable for finding the system's breaking points, but the scenarios may be unrealistically adversarial. Filter adversarial scenarios for plausibility: only keep scenarios that could actually occur in the operational design domain.

steps.description: Construct the statistical argument that the autonomous system is acceptably safe: define the safety target, compute the required test volume, and assess the residual risk.

inputs.name: scenario-library
inputs.desc: Test scenarios with results

inputs.name: validation-objectives
inputs.desc: Safety target and confidence level

outputs.name: safety-argument
outputs.desc: Statistical safety argument with evidence, assumptions, and residual risk quantification

outputs.name: test-completeness
outputs.desc: Assessment of whether sufficient testing has been performed to support the safety claim

process: Define the safety target. Common formulation: the system shall have a fatality rate below X per mile (or per hour). The target is often derived from human driver performance: the system must be at least as safe as an attentive human driver, or N times safer. In the US, the human fatality rate is approximately 1.1 per 100 million miles. A target of 10x safer requires demonstrating a rate below 0.11 per 100 million miles. This is the statistical challenge: proving a very low rate requires enormous evidence.

Compute the required test volume for a purely statistical argument. To demonstrate a failure rate below lambda with confidence C, you need approximately -ln(1-C)/lambda miles (or scenarios) with zero failures. For lambda = 10^-8 per mile (10x safer than human) at 95% confidence: need 3*10^8 miles. This is infeasible with real-world driving alone (billions of miles). This is why simulation is essential: accelerate testing by running millions of scenarios in simulation, each representing a miles-equivalent of driving.

Construct a structured safety argument that combines evidence types. Pure mileage-based argument: we drove/simulated N miles with zero fatalities, therefore the rate is below X. Scenario-based argument: we tested all scenario types in the ODD, each with parameter variation, and the system passed all. Analysis-based argument: the system architecture has redundancy and fault detection that provides a calculated residual risk below the target. Combine these into a multi-pronged argument: simulation covers breadth (millions of scenarios), real-world testing validates that simulation results transfer, analysis fills gaps where testing cannot reach. The argument is stronger when all three prongs agree.

Assess residual risk and known limitations. After all testing and analysis, quantify the residual risk: the probability that the system encounters a scenario it cannot handle, multiplied by the probability of harm. The residual risk includes: scenarios in ODD Area 3 (unknown hazardous, see SOTIF analysis), hardware failures not covered by redundancy, environmental conditions beyond the ODD that the system fails to detect and reject. Document these honestly. The safety case is an argument, not a proof; it must be transparent about what is known, what is assumed, and what remains uncertain.

description: Design the human-robot interaction system: build situational awareness interfaces, implement teleoperation with shared autonomy, design mode switching and handoff protocols, and ensure physical interaction safety.

steps.description: Design the interface that communicates the robot's state and intent to human operators or bystanders: what the robot perceives, what it plans to do, and how confident it is.

inputs.name: robot-system
inputs.desc: The autonomous system with its perception, planning, and control capabilities

inputs.name: user-roles
inputs.desc: Who interacts with the robot (operator, supervisor, bystander, co-worker) and what they need to know

outputs.name: interface-design
outputs.desc: Interface layout and information architecture for each user role

outputs.name: information-priority-model
outputs.desc: What to show and when, based on urgency and relevance

process: Identify what information each user role needs. Operator (remote): full perception view (camera feeds, lidar visualization), system status (localization confidence, sensor health, battery, connectivity), current plan (trajectory, next action), and alerts (detected anomalies, approaching limits). Supervisor (oversight): aggregate fleet status, individual robot status on demand, exception alerts, intervention history. Bystander: the robot's immediate intent (direction of travel, stopping, yielding) through physical signals (lights, sounds, display). Co-worker (collaborative robot): the robot's planned motion (will it enter my workspace), force/speed status, e-stop accessibility.

Design the display hierarchy. Apply the visual hierarchy: most critical information largest and most prominent, secondary information available but not distracting. For remote operation: center of display is the primary camera view or map view, periphery shows system health indicators, bottom shows the current action and next planned action. Use color coding consistently: green for nominal, yellow for degraded, red for fault or alert. Avoid information overload: show summary status by default, drill-down for details. Display confidence levels for perception outputs so the operator knows when to trust or override.

Design intent communication for bystanders and co-workers. External signals: LED strips showing direction of travel (animated directional pattern), brake lights for deceleration, warning lights for reversing. Audio: low tone for normal operation (so people know it is there), higher tone or verbal announcement for approaching people or tight spaces. Display: a simple screen showing the robot's immediate plan in pictographic form (arrow for direction, stop sign for stopping). For collaborative robots: projected light showing the planned workspace boundary on the floor.

Prioritize information by urgency. Define alert levels: informational (system status changes, logged for review), advisory (approaching a limitation, operator should be aware), caution (action may be needed soon), warning (immediate action required). Each alert level gets progressively more intrusive display: informational updates in a log, advisory as a highlighted status change, caution as a pop-up with audio tone, warning as a full-screen alert with persistent audio. Test with operators to verify that critical information is noticed and non-critical information does not cause alarm fatigue.

steps.description: Implement teleoperation with shared autonomy: handle communication latency, blend human input with autonomous capability, and design the control interface for efficient remote operation.

inputs.name: robot-system
inputs.desc: Robot with its autonomous capabilities and communication link

inputs.name: interface-design
inputs.desc: Operator interface layout

outputs.name: teleoperation-system
outputs.desc: Teleoperation control system with latency compensation and shared autonomy modes

outputs.name: operator-workload-analysis
outputs.desc: Analysis of operator cognitive load and maximum number of robots per operator

process: Characterize the communication link. Measure: round-trip latency (typical: 50-200ms for cellular, 500ms-2s for satellite), jitter (variation in latency), bandwidth (sufficient for video and control data), reliability (packet loss rate). Latency above 300ms makes direct teleoperation (joystick to motor) unreliable due to operator overcorrection. Above 1s, direct teleoperation is impractical. The communication link quality determines the level of autonomy sharing required.

Design shared autonomy levels. Level 1 (direct teleoperation): operator sends velocity or steering commands, robot executes immediately. Viable only with <200ms latency. Level 2 (assisted teleoperation): operator sends high-level commands (go to waypoint, follow path), robot handles low-level control (obstacle avoidance, path following). Viable up to ~1s latency. Level 3 (supervisory control): robot operates autonomously, operator monitors and intervenes by exception (approve a decision, select an alternative plan). Viable for any latency. Level 4 (full autonomy with escalation): robot operates independently, escalates specific decisions to the operator when it is uncertain. Implement seamless transitions between levels based on link quality and situation complexity.

Implement latency compensation. Predictive display: render the robot's predicted future state (where it will be given the current commands and vehicle model) alongside the actual state. The operator controls the predicted state, which feels responsive despite the delayed feedback. Model-based: maintain a local simulation of the robot on the operator's side, driven by the same commands; the local simulation provides instant feedback while the real robot catches up. Haptic feedback: if using force-feedback controls, model the remote environment locally and update with delayed sensor data; direct force transmission over a latent link causes instability.

Analyze operator workload. Count the information sources the operator must monitor and the decisions they must make per unit time. For a single robot in a complex environment: one operator is fully occupied. For robots in simple environments with high autonomy: one operator can supervise 3-5 robots (fleet management model). Key factor: the intervention rate. If the robot needs operator input every 30 seconds, one operator per robot. If the robot needs input every 10 minutes, one operator can handle a small fleet. Measure intervention rates from field data and staff accordingly.

steps.description: Design mode switching between manual, assisted, and autonomous operation: define transition criteria, manage handoff timing, and prevent mode confusion.

inputs.name: teleoperation-system
inputs.desc: Teleoperation and shared autonomy capabilities

inputs.name: robot-system
inputs.desc: Autonomous system capabilities and limitations

outputs.name: mode-switching-design
outputs.desc: Mode transition logic, handoff timing, and mode annunciation design

outputs.name: mode-confusion-mitigations
outputs.desc: Analysis and mitigations for mode confusion risks

process: Define the operating modes and their capabilities. Manual: human has direct control, robot provides no autonomous assistance. Assisted: human controls with robot assistance (e.g., collision avoidance active, speed limiting). Autonomous: robot controls, human monitors. Emergency: robot executes a predefined safe behavior regardless of human input. Each mode must have clear entry conditions, exit conditions, and annunciation (visual and auditory indication of the current mode).

Design the handoff protocol for human-to-robot transition. When the operator engages autonomous mode: verify all preconditions (sensors healthy, localization valid, mission loaded), display a confirmation with the autonomous system's plan, require explicit operator confirmation (button press with verification), ramp control authority from operator to robot over 1-2 seconds (not instant) to smooth the transition. The operator must confirm they are monitoring; passive engagement (not touching controls does not mean monitoring) must be detected and flagged.

Design the handoff protocol for robot-to-human transition. The robot escalates to the human when: it encounters a situation outside its capability, a fault reduces its confidence below the threshold, or the operator requests control. The escalation must provide: time budget (how long before the robot must act without human input), context (what the situation is, what options the robot sees), a default action (what the robot will do if the human does not respond). The human must have enough time and information to make a decision. If the human does not respond within the time budget, the robot executes the default (which must be safe, not optimal).

Mitigate mode confusion. Mode confusion occurs when the human and robot disagree about who is in control. Historical cause of accidents in aviation and autonomous driving. Mitigations: always annunciate the current mode prominently (large indicator, distinct colors), require positive action to change modes (no automatic mode transitions without operator awareness), maintain control input monitoring (if the operator provides input inconsistent with the current mode, alert them), log all mode transitions for post-incident analysis. Test the mode switching design with human subjects to identify confusion scenarios before deployment.

outputs.name: risk-assessment
outputs.desc: Contact scenario analysis with force/pressure calculations against ISO/TS 15066 limits

process: Identify contact scenarios. Transient contact: the robot strikes a person and the person can move away (quasi-static impact followed by retraction). Quasi-static contact: the person is trapped between the robot and a fixed object (clamping). For each scenario, identify: the body region that could be contacted (head, chest, hand, leg), the effective mass of the robot at the contact point (from the manipulator dynamics and configuration), and the relative velocity at impact.

Calculate contact forces and pressures. For transient contact, the impact force depends on the effective mass of the robot at the contact point and the impact velocity: F = sqrt(k * m_reduced * v^2) where k is the contact stiffness (depends on body region, from ISO/TS 15066 Annex A) and m_reduced is the reduced mass (robot effective mass in series with body mass). For quasi-static contact, the force is determined by the robot's maximum force output in the trapped direction. Calculate the resulting pressure from the contact area (robot surface geometry).

Compare against ISO/TS 15066 biomechanical limits. The standard provides maximum permissible force and pressure for each body region, for both transient and quasi-static contact. Example: for the hand (transient), maximum force is 130 N and maximum pressure is 160 N/cm^2. If the calculated force or pressure exceeds the limit, implement mitigation: reduce robot speed (lower impact velocity), add padding (larger contact area, lower pressure, lower contact stiffness), reduce payload (lower effective mass), restrict workspace to avoid trapping scenarios.

Design the protective stop system. Safety-rated monitored stop: the robot stops all motion when a person enters the collaborative workspace, uses safety-rated sensors (safety laser scanner, light curtain, safety-rated camera). Speed and separation monitoring: the robot dynamically adjusts its speed based on the distance to the nearest person, stopping before a collision could exceed the force limit. Power and force limiting: the robot operates at forces below the biomechanical limits at all times, using compliant actuators, joint torque sensing, or external force/torque sensors. Select the method based on the task: power/force limiting allows continuous collaboration, monitored stop is simpler but stops production when humans are near.
